terms.d: TEA, Johari, PE Scale, esteem/efficacy/respect, assertiveness.
ICEDIP, Six Hats, cognitive flexibility and errors.
Schemas, attribution, stereotype vs prejudice.

concepts: Walk the map: Self → thinking tools → social cognition.
Faculty often weight Module 2 (EI/attitudes) higher than Module 1 foundations.
Many Module 1 LMR items are definition + contrast pairs.
notes: Open each card’s Deep notes for term lists and exam traps.
LMR cards (orange outline) are denser — prioritise those for revision.

terms.d: Evaluation of a person, idea, or object as favourable or unfavourable.
Interpret, understand, and manage own and others’ emotions at work.
Affective · Behavioural · Cognitive — not Ellis ABC.

concepts: Exam-heavy module: attitude structure + Goleman EI usually outweigh Module 1 alone.
Attitude ABC ≠ Ellis ABC (Module 5: Adversity–Beliefs–Consequences).
EI (self + others) ≠ Gardner intrapersonal (self only).
notes: If a stem mixes ABC flavours, check which module frame it is asking for.
Locus of control (internal/external) is a live-class extra — useful in case answers.

terms.d: Incompatible goals, cognitions, or emotions leading to opposition.
Neutral facilitation — not taking sides or judging.
Distributive (claim value) vs integrative (create value).

concepts: Flow: diagnose conflict → choose style → mediate if needed → negotiate.
Disagreement ≠ full conflict; conflict is not always negative.
Four pillars sit on top of negotiation technique.
notes: Match resolution style to stakes and time (compete vs collaborate vs avoid).
Mediator ≠ arbitrator who decides for the parties.

terms.d: Terminal = desired ends; instrumental = preferred means/modes of behaviour.
Positive adaptation in the face of serious adversity — both parts required.
Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity.

concepts: Ethics applies standards to conduct; values shape what is desirable.
Ellis ABC (beliefs mediate feelings) ≠ Attitude ABC.
Agility adapts behaviour under VUCA; resilience adapts under adversity.
notes: Resilience stems need both adversity and positive adaptation.
Rokeach: responsibility as means to friendship = instrumental serving terminal.

terms.d: Sense of personal identity; studied via person–situation interaction.
Affective, Behavioural, Cognitive domains of the self.
Knowledge representation about oneself — traits, roles, values — organised into self-schemas.
Mental structure that guides processing of self-relevant information.

concepts: Self-concept is cognitive self-knowledge; it is not the same as self-esteem (global worth).
ABCs here describe domains of the self — different from Attitude ABC and Ellis ABC.
Schemas about the self filter what you notice and remember about yourself.
notes: Stem “knowledge about oneself / self-schemas” → self-concept.
Stem “global worth / liking yourself” → self-esteem (1.5), not self-concept.
Don’t answer Attitude ABC when the stem is about the self’s ABCs.

terms.d: Thoughts, Emotions, and Actions constantly influence each other.
Internal processing and beliefs.
Internal states and felt values.
External behaviours and words.

concepts: Changing one TEA component tends to shift the others — reciprocal, not one-way.
Useful for coaching/case answers: intervene at thought, feeling, or behaviour level.
Related to but not identical with Attitude ABC (evaluation components) or Ellis ABC (adversity→beliefs→consequences).
notes: LMR: “mutual influence / change one shifts others” → TEA.
If stem lists Affective–Behavioural–Cognitive as attitude parts → Module 2, not TEA.
If stem is Adversity–Beliefs–Consequences → Ellis (5.4), not TEA.
One-line exam answer: Thoughts, emotions, and actions continually influence each other.

terms.d: Four panes of known/unknown information to self and others (Luft & Ingham).
Known to self and known to others.
Known to others, unknown to self.
Known to self, unknown to others.
Unknown to self and unknown to others.

concepts: Enlarge Open by feedback (shrink Blind) + disclosure (shrink Hidden).
Trust grows when disclosure and learning from feedback work together.
PE Scale (1.4) are skills that operate on Johari panes — they are not the four panes themselves.
notes: LMR: “others know / you don’t” → Blind; “you know / others don’t” → Hidden.
Listing panes without Unknown is a common miss.
Don’t confuse Johari panes with PE Scale dimensions (SD, OTF, Perceptiveness).
Stem “enlarge the Arena” → feedback + disclosure.

terms.d: Personal Effectiveness: Self-disclosure (SD), Openness to feedback (OTF), Perceptiveness.
Willingness to share relevant self-information.
Willingness to receive and use others’ observations.
Ability to notice cues about self, others, and situations.

concepts: Effective people use SD + OTF + perceptiveness to shrink secret/blind areas and enlarge the Arena.
PE dimensions act on Johari — they are tools, not the pane names.
Low SD + low OTF keeps people stuck with large Hidden/Blind areas.
notes: Stem asks for three PE dimensions → SD, OTF, Perceptiveness.
If options are Open/Blind/Hidden/Unknown → Johari, not PE Scale.
Link answer to Johari when asked how PE improves the Open area.

terms.d: Overall subjective sense of personal worth / liking of self.
Belief you can succeed at a specific task or goal — not a global trait.
Pride in who you are, moral courage, and standards for how you allow yourself to be treated.
Cognitive map of who you are (see 1.1) — distinct from esteem and efficacy.

concepts: Esteem = global worth; efficacy = task-specific confidence; respect = dignity/treatment standards.
You can have high esteem but low efficacy on a hard exam task (or the reverse).
Faculty often test the esteem vs efficacy contrast with one concrete example.
notes: LMR: “task-specific belief I can do X” → self-efficacy.
LMR: “overall worth / like myself” → self-esteem.
Don’t use self-concept when the stem is about worth or task confidence.
One example ready: “I value myself (esteem) but doubt I can code this module (low efficacy).”

terms.d: Express thoughts/feelings truthfully while respecting others — between passivity and aggression.
Withhold needs; avoid conflict at personal cost.
Push needs without respect for others.
Respect, Openness, Honesty, Accountability, Self-control, Delegation.

concepts: Assertive ≠ aggressive: honesty plus respect is the differentiator.
Delegation appears in the assertive skills list — not only a management technique.
Links to EI (Module 2): self-regulation and social skill support assertiveness.
notes: LMR: “between passive and aggressive” → assertiveness.
Be ready to list 4–6 skills if asked (ROHASD mnemonic: Respect, Openness, Honesty, Accountability, Self-control, Delegation).
If stem rewards “winning at all costs” → competing/aggression, not assertiveness.

terms.d: Respectful communication, privacy awareness, and appropriate sharing online.
How thoughtfully people take up tools in ways that affect reputation and norms.

concepts: Online presence is part of workplace reputation — etiquette is professional behaviour, not optional manners.
Oversharing and ignoring organisational norms are classic exam “wrong” cues.
notes: Stem emphasises privacy / respectful posting / appropriate sharing → etiquette.
Don’t answer with maximum authenticity-via-oversharing.

terms.d: Inspiration, Clarification, Distillation, Perspiration, Evaluation, Incubation.
Stepping away so subconscious processing can occur.
Judging strengths and flaws — not the same as incubation.
Mental rehearsal: combine outcome + process simulation; participant > observer perspective.

concepts: ICEDIP phases can occur in any order and repeat; each phase has its own mind-set.
Incubation ≠ evaluation — frequent mix-up.
Visualization works better when you rehearse steps (process) not only the trophy (outcome).
notes: LMR: expand all six ICEDIP letters once under exam pressure.
“Step away / subconscious” → Incubation; “judge quality” → Evaluation.
Visualization: participant perspective generally beats observer perspective.
Order rule: any order, repeatable — don’t invent a fixed sequence as the only truth.

terms.d: Capacity to notice when something is wrong or likely to go wrong.

concepts: Sensitivity = recognition only; it does not include solving the problem.
Distinct from cognitive flexibility (adapting strategies) and from Six Hats (structured thinking modes).
notes: Stem “notice only / not solve” → problem sensitivity.
If options include fixing the issue, that is problem solving — not sensitivity.

terms.d: Process control — director of the thinking agenda.
Facts and data only — no spin.
Feelings and intuition — no justification required in the moment.
Risks, caution, critical flaws — detached risk analysis.
Benefits and optimism.
Creativity and alternatives.

concepts: Hats are parallel thinking modes — one mode at a time, not personality labels forever.
Blue is meta-control: manages when other hats are used.
Black ≠ “being a bad person”; it is disciplined caution.
notes: LMR: map colour → function cold (Blue/White/Red/Black/Yellow/Green).
“Facts only / detective” → White; “feelings” → Red; “risks” → Black; “ideas” → Green.
Blue hat ≠ content expert — it runs the process.
Don’t confuse hat colours with Tuckman stages or conflict styles.

terms.d: Disengage from one task, hold several concepts, adapt strategies to new conditions — learnable.
Seeing only extremes; no middle ground.
One event becomes a forever rule.
Dwelling on one negative detail.
“I feel it, therefore it is true.”
Assuming others’ thoughts or predicting catastrophe as fact.

concepts: SLM packs flexibility with Beck/Burns cognitive errors as one exam cluster.
Flexibility is executive-function skill; errors are biased thinking patterns — related but not identical.
Emotional reasoning is a high-yield named error with a one-line example.
notes: LMR: name 4–5 errors with a tiny example each (especially emotional reasoning, all-or-nothing).
“I feel anxious so the project is failing” → emotional reasoning.
Flexibility stem focuses on adapting / switching sets, not listing biases.
Don’t dump Six Hats colours as “cognitive errors.”

terms.d: How people perceive, recall, attend to, and use social information.
Mental structure of general knowledge about a social object or situation.
How much a cue stands out and grabs attention.
Recent exposure makes a schema more accessible.
Inferring intentions, desires, emotions, traits from observed behaviour.

concepts: Salience and priming both raise schema accessibility — different routes.
Social inference supports social success; it is part of the social cognition family.
Attribution (1.13) is a specialised form of causal inference about behaviour.
notes: “Recent exposure makes idea come to mind” → priming.
Don’t answer FAE when the stem is only about schemas/priming.

terms.d: Inferring causes of behaviour.
Personality, ability, effort.
Environment, luck, others’ actions.
For others: overestimate personal causes, underestimate situation.
For self as actor: emphasise external causes more than when observing others.
Credit success internally; blame failure externally.

concepts: FAE targets explanations of others; actor–observer is about self vs other perspectives; self-serving protects self-image.
All three are attribution biases — learn the trio as a set.
Internal vs external is the basic causal split before biases.
notes: LMR trio: FAE · actor–observer · self-serving — one line each.
“He failed because he’s lazy” (ignoring context) → FAE.
“I failed because the exam was unfair” after “I passed because I’m smart” → self-serving.
Don’t swap FAE with self-serving when the stem is about judging other people.

terms.d: Cognitive generalization about a group (“pictures in our heads”).
Derogatory / evaluative attitude toward group members.
Behaviour — unfair treatment based on group membership.
Intergroup contact can reduce prejudice via knowledge, lower anxiety, empathy.

concepts: Stereotype = cognitive; prejudice = evaluative attitude; discrimination = behaviour.
Prejudice is not automatically the same as discriminatory acts.
Accepting criticism skills (calm, restate, open perspectives) are packed on this map card with S-P-D.
notes: LMR: “generalized idea about a group” → stereotype; “negative attitude” → prejudice; “unequal treatment” → discrimination.
Contact reduces prejudice by knowledge + empathy + lower anxiety — not by increasing distance.
Criticism steps: remain calm → reiterate (“So you’re saying…”) → open both views → polite exit if needed.
Don’t call prejudice a behaviour; that’s discrimination.

terms.d: Evaluation of a person, idea, or object as favourable or unfavourable.

concepts: Attitudes are evaluative orientations that influence perception and behaviour (Allport’s centrality in social psychology).
Attitude object = whatever is being evaluated.
notes: Definition stem → evaluation, not a Tuckman stage or sociometric pattern.

terms.d: Magnitude of favourability or unfavourability.
Number of components in the attitude system (simple vs complex).
Importance of the object to the person; central attitudes resist change.
Attitudes show up across domains via socialization.
Inferred from effects; learned over life (often family-transmitted).

concepts: Characteristics pack: valence, multiplicity, needs served, centrality, pervasiveness, invisible, acquired.
High centrality → hard to change; useful for persuasion and change questions.
Valence is strength of +/−, not the same as multiplicity (how many pieces).
notes: LMR: “strength of favour/unfavour” → valence; “importance / resists change” → centrality.
Be ready to explain needs, pervasiveness, invisible, acquired in one line each.
Don’t confuse valence with VI (Idealized Influence) or with emotion intensity alone.

terms.d: Beliefs and knowledge about the attitude object.
Feelings toward the object.
Action tendency / how one tends to act.

concepts: Attitude ABC = Affective–Behavioural–Cognitive evaluation structure.
Ellis ABC (Module 5) is Adversity–Beliefs–Consequences — different model, similar letters.
Belief statement (“discrimination is wrong”) is mainly cognitive; anger about it is affective.
notes: LMR: map stem language to A/B/C carefully.
If Adversity/Activating event appears → Ellis, not Attitude ABC.
TEA (1.2) is thoughts–emotions–actions influence, not the attitude ABC triad.

terms.d: Powerful, often triggered, more intentional affective state.
Prolonged, less intense, not necessarily triggered; may lack intentionality.
Less intense/lasting; life can continue.
High intensity, long duration, hard to control, disrupts daily life.

concepts: SLM does not say “positive = good / negative = useless” — intensity, duration, and control matter.
Self-awareness of emotion underpins EI (2.5).
notes: Emotion vs mood: intensity + trigger + intentionality.
Unhealthy ≠ simply “negative feeling.”

terms.d: Interpret, reason about, understand, and manage own and others’ emotions; stay stable and communicate.
Know your emotions as they happen.
Think before acting; manage disruptive impulses.
Drive toward goals with energy and persistence.
Understand others’ feelings.
Manage relationships and build networks.

concepts: Goleman five: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
Personal competence = awareness/regulation/motivation; social competence = empathy + social skills.
Faculty: EI usually outweighs interpersonal intelligence alone for exam priority.
notes: LMR: list all five competencies cold.
Sociometric starring / Tuckman / hat colours are not EI competencies.
EI spans self and others; intrapersonal (2.6) focuses on self.

terms.d: Understand others’ minds; communicate; form and sustain relationships.
Understand oneself — interests, fears, abilities — and manage one’s life.

concepts: Interpersonal = others; intrapersonal = self; EI covers both with emotion focus.
Self-awareness underpins intrapersonal skill and EI.
Exam priority cue from faculty: EI > interpersonal intelligence alone.
notes: “Understanding myself to manage my life” → intrapersonal.
“Reading others / rapport / social comfort” → interpersonal.
If stem asks which faculty prioritises → EI over interpersonal alone.

terms.d: Incompatible goals, cognitions, or emotions within/between people or groups.
Incompatible desired outcomes.
Incompatible ideas or interpretations.
Incompatible emotions (e.g. anger between people).
Conditions with potential for conflict before open clash.
Open antagonistic behaviour.

concepts: Stages often framed: Latent → Perceived → Felt → Manifest.
Conflict is common and not always negative — resolution can yield constructive problem solving.
Sources include unclear responsibilities, poor processes, communication problems.
notes: “Incompatible feelings / anger at each other” → affective conflict.
“Conditions exist but no open fight yet” → latent.
Disagreement alone ≠ full conflict until opposition escalates.

terms.d: Can harm trust/performance — or spur creativity if managed.
e.g. unrealistic goals that tempt cutting corners; toxic culture; misuse of time/tech.

concepts: Impact is two-sided: damage vs constructive tension.
Goal pressure is a classic ethics risk in conflict settings.
notes: Unrealistic targets + corner-cutting → ethical dilemma framing.
Don’t answer “conflict is always good.”

terms.d: High assertiveness, low cooperativeness — win at all costs.
High assertiveness and cooperativeness — seek win–win.
Moderate on both — split the difference.
Low assertiveness and cooperativeness — sidestep.
Low assertiveness, high cooperativeness — yield.

concepts: Match style to stakes: outcome-critical → competing; relationship + outcome → collaborate/compromise.
Little time → avoiding / competing / accommodating; lots of time → collaborate / compromise.
Styles are tools, not personality forever.
notes: “Win at all costs / highly assertive, uncooperative” → competing.
Relationship + outcome + time allows → collaborate or compromise.
Don’t pick collaborating when the stem says emergency with no time.

terms.d: Neutral facilitator helps parties; does not take sides or impose a verdict.
What people truly need vs the demands they state.
Culture shapes how disagreement, face-saving, and decisions are expressed.

concepts: Mediator keeps process fair, focuses on interests, avoids blame, helps generate options.
Preconditions: willingness to participate and a workable setting.
Misreading cultural cues can escalate conflict.
notes: Mediator ≠ judge or partisan advocate.
Intercultural awareness is communication skill inside conflict resolution, not a separate “hat.”

terms.d: Claim value — fixed pie.
Create value — expand joint gains.
Often preparation → exchange/bargaining → closing → implementation.

concepts: Purpose includes agreements, contracts, and solving joint problems.
Integrative seeks mutual gains; distributive divides a limited resource.
notes: “Expand joint gains / mutual value” → integrative.
“Split a fixed amount” → distributive.

terms.d: Build productive relationships (Comprehend–Anticipate–Connect).
Pursue outcomes, not debating points.
Shift from “your way/my way” to shared needs.
Agreements people will carry out voluntarily.

concepts: Persuasion, professional conduct, and clear closing support follow-through.
Fairness and relationship quality affect whether deals stick.
notes: “Pursue outcomes, not points” = check whether terms advance real goals.
Comprehend–Anticipate–Connect → relationship pillar, not Black-hat criticism.

terms.d: Fundamental beliefs directing desirable behaviour or end states.
Desired end outcomes (e.g. freedom, true friendship).
Preferred modes of behaviour/means (e.g. responsibility, independence).
Moral right/wrong and codes of conduct (from ethos, “character”).

concepts: Instrumental values help reach terminal ends (means → ends).
Values shape what is desirable; ethics judges right conduct — related but distinct.
Organisations encode both in mission, vision, and policies.
notes: LMR: terminal = ends; instrumental = means.
“Being responsible to achieve true friendship” → instrumental serving terminal.
Don’t confuse Rokeach types with Attitude valence or Tuckman stages.

terms.d: Empathy, honesty, courage, commitment.
Respect, responsibility, integrity, care, harmony.

concepts: Moral values and moral icons support character / “new self-awareness.”
Core values list is a frequent recall item.
notes: Core values set: respect, responsibility, integrity, care, harmony.
Don’t substitute Tuckman stage names for core values.

terms.d: Dynamic positive adaptation in the face of serious adversity.
Acute crises or chronic low-intensity workplace stress.

concepts: Definition requires both adversity experience and positive adaptation.
Viewed as trait, developable capability, and/or process.
Links to EI, networks (5.5), and agility (5.6) without being identical to them.
notes: LMR: both adversity + positive adaptation must appear in the answer.
High valence attitudes alone ≠ resilience.
Sociometric star ≠ resilience definition.

terms.d: Many options can overwhelm decisions and reduce satisfaction.
Adversity/Activating event → Beliefs → Consequences (emotions/behaviours).

concepts: Beliefs mediate reactions — events alone do not fully determine feelings.
Ellis ABC ≠ Attitude ABC (affective–behavioural–cognitive).
Choice paradox is a coping/uncertainty theme beside Ellis.
notes: LMR: B = Beliefs in Ellis ABC.
Attitude ABC centres on evaluation components; Ellis centres on beliefs about adversity.
Don’t answer Blue hat or branding for Ellis “B.”

terms.d: Personality/cognitive variables, family/social networks, work demands and resources.
Coping skills, support, and resource building.

concepts: Family and social networks are framed as supports that can promote resilience.
Stress shows models, symptoms, consequences — management is resource-based.
notes: Networks in Unit 5.2 framing = resilience-promoting supports, not irrelevant.
Don’t treat networks only as FAE sources.

terms.d: Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity, Ambiguity.
Adapting methods and behaviours under turbulent, unpredictable conditions.
e.g. Vision as a response pairing to Volatility.

concepts: Agility answers VUCA; resilience answers adversity — complementary.
U in VUCA = Uncertainty (not Utility/Urgency alone).
notes: “U” → Uncertainty.
Agility ≠ refusing change; ≠ only competing conflict style.
Don’t enlarge Hidden Johari pane as an agility answer.

terms.d: People working together for shared goals with commitment to a vision.
Pattern of how a leader influences and directs others.
Measuring interpersonal choice/relatedness in a group (Moreno).

concepts: Flow on this map: Teams → Leadership → Excellence tools.
Exam cluster: Tuckman + situational leadership + sociometry patterns show up often.
notes: Use Deep notes on each card for definitions and traps.
LMR cards (orange outline) carry denser notes.

terms.d: Interdependent members pursuing common goals/purpose with shared vision.
Who is on the team — skills, knowledge, abilities, other characteristics (KSAOs).
Visible differences (e.g. demographics) — effects often fade over time.
Values, personality, attitudes — often matter longer term.
How much members must rely on each other; higher interdependence → stronger need for real teamwork.

concepts: Design levers: composition + roles + task characteristics.
Roles are often clarified during storming, not only at kickoff.
Deep-level diversity ≠ surface-level; exam likes the longer-term impact of deep-level.
notes: Don’t answer “diversity” without saying surface vs deep when asked.
Team ≠ people sitting near each other; look for shared purpose + interdependence.

terms.d: Five-stage team life cycle describing how groups develop over time (plus later Adjourning).
Orientation and politeness; members test boundaries; high dependence on leader and structure.
Conflict and assertiveness; challenges to leadership; roles and power often sorted here.
Cohesion and trust grow; shared norms and group maintenance become clearer.
Strong task focus; high functioning; less day-to-day dependence on the leader.
Team disbands; closure, recognition, and emotional wind-down (celebrate / let go).

concepts: Fixed exam order: Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning.
Storming ≠ failure: conflict is expected while roles and influence settle.
Norming vs Performing: Norming builds the social glue; Performing converts that glue into output.
Leader load falls across stages: high structure early → more facilitation later → less needed in Performing.
Lifecycle can recycle: new members, new goals, or crises can push a performing team back toward storming/norming.
Link to team design (3.1): composition sets who enters forming; roles often become clear in storming.
notes: One-word cues: polite → Forming · conflict → Storming · trust/norms → Norming · task/output → Performing · goodbye → Adjourning.
Stem says “challenge leadership / disagreement / assertiveness” → Storming.
Stem says “cohesion / shared norms / trust” → Norming (not Performing unless task results are emphasised).
Listing stages without Adjourning is a common miss — tuck it on the end.
Don’t confuse Tuckman stages with Lewin styles or Blanchard S1–S4 (those are leadership frames, not team phases).
If asked “is storming bad?” — answer: normal stage; unmanaged conflict is the problem, not the stage itself.

terms.d: Uses type/preference tools (e.g. MBTI) to improve understanding.
Shared tasks/experiences to build bonds and cooperation.
Targets specific team skills (communication, coordination).
Uses real or simulated problems to improve process together.

concepts: Team building is intentional development work — not only social events.
Performance issues often sit in roles, trust, or process — building aims at those gaps.
Match type of building to the diagnosis (skill gap vs trust gap vs process gap).
notes: MBTI workshop → personality-based (classic MCQ cue).
Don’t confuse team building types with Tuckman stages.

terms.d: Impact rises: Managerial → Relational → Motivational → Inspirational → Transformational (develops other leaders).
Leader holds control; little subordinate initiative.
Consultation and mutual consensus; can slow decisions.
Maximum independence; leader helps when asked.

concepts: Two frames in one topic: (1) types-by-impact ladder, (2) Lewin’s three styles.
Lewin styles are about how decisions/control are shared — not the same list as Bass 4 Is.
Democratic ≠ slow always, but SLM notes consensus can take time.
notes: “Help only when asked / max independence” → laissez-faire.
Don’t mix Lewin trio with Blanchard S1–S4 (that’s 3.6).

terms.d: Vision, enthusiasm, meaning that energises followers.
Challenges assumptions; encourages new thinking.
Role-model / charismatic trust and respect.
Coaches and develops people as individuals.
Exchange, monitoring, rewards/corrective action; short-term planning; useful in emergencies or clear gain–exchange settings.

concepts: Transformational develops and inspires; transactional manages exchanges and compliance.
Both can appear in practice — not always either/or.
4 Is are the high-yield list — Individualized Consideration is a frequent MCQ distractor vs PE Scale / Tuckman.
notes: Mnemonic tip: IM · IS · Idealized · Individualized.
If answer options mix Tuckman and 4 Is, pick the leadership frame.

terms.d: No single best style — match leader behaviour to follower readiness/development and the situation.
High directive / low supportive — for low competence, high commitment (enthusiastic beginner).
High directive / high supportive — competence growing; still needs direction plus persuasion.
Low directive / high supportive — capable but variable commitment; share decisions.
Low directive / low supportive — high competence and high commitment.
Combination of competence and commitment (development level).

concepts: Core claim: adapt style — positional power alone is outdated.
Match table: low competence + high commitment → S1; high competence + high commitment → S4.
Goleman’s six styles (coaching, pacesetting, democratic, affiliative, authoritative, coercive) is a related “situational” menu — don’t confuse with S1–S4 labels.
Contrast with Lewin (fixed style labels) and with transformational 4 Is (qualities), not readiness matching.
notes: LMR: if stem gives competence + commitment, map straight to S1–S4.
“No one best style” is the slogan answer for situational leadership.
Don’t pick S4 Delegating for a novice who is still keen — that’s S1.
Keep Lewin / Bass / Blanchard in separate mental drawers.

terms.d: Measurement of interpersonal relatedness and choice patterns (socius + metrum).
Visual map of who chooses whom / network links.
Table of choices between members.
Person most often chosen for a given criterion (hub).
Little or no choice links — peripheral in the network.
Democratic multi-link pattern (many reciprocal/cross links).
Hub-and-spoke / more authoritarian choice structure.
Awareness → Desire → Knowledge → Ability → Reinforcement — stages so change sticks.

concepts: Strategic leadership themes: mentoring, trust, guiding people through change.
Sociometry is diagnostic of group structure — not the same as Johari panes.
Star vs net: hub concentration vs distributed democratic links — exam contrast.
Change stages explain adoption; sociometry explains relationships inside the group.
notes: LMR: star = most chosen; isolate = least connected; net = multi-link democratic.
If asked for Moreno / sociogram / criterion choices → sociometry, not Tuckman.
Don’t confuse sociometric star with transformational Idealized Influence.
Remember ADKAR order if change stages are asked; prioritise sociometry patterns when both appear.

terms.d: Strategic positioning of a positive, differentiated self-image/narrative for a target audience; needs introspection.
Plan, goals, deadlines, delegation; allocate right time via important vs urgent.
Traditional framing: keep domains separated.
Prioritising and blending work and personal aspects of identity — SLM treats this as more realistic than hard separation.
Healthy relationships can raise productivity and lower turnover when guided by policy and discreet managerial skill.

concepts: Branding is intentional narrative, not only “being yourself online.”
Integration vs balance is a favourite compare-contrast: blend vs separate.
Time skill = prioritisation (important/urgent), not only working longer hours.
Relationship management links excellence tools back to leadership/climate.
notes: LMR: integration ≠ balance — say “blend identities” vs “rigid separation.”
Important vs urgent → time management cue.
Personal branding needs a target audience + differentiation, not generic positivity.
Bundle reminder: this card packs four themes — answer the stem’s focus (brand / time / integration / relationships).
